Chemometrics Engineering Report · CDA Star-Map Suite

Fable Enhances Contrast of idws vs idcn Algorithms

A field mystery, a fresh visualization lens, and the invention of a smoother confidence engine — the origin story of idcn, reenacted end-to-end in CDA_mapstar_Merge_new.m
JULY 9, 2026 · HDPE / LDPE / PVC · 119 WAVELENGTH VARIABLES · CLAUDE (FABLE 5) FOR OLD BEAR

Executive Summary

Every classification bug story begins the same way: the field notices before the lab does. The company’s field application engineers reported predictions that made no geometric sense — samples of one class, sitting between correctly identified neighbors of the same class, condemned as something else entirely. All the field could see was the verdicts; the reason was invisible. It happened that Old Bear was then building a class-map visualization tool, patterned after the commercial graphing package SigmaPlot. Pointing that fresh lens at the data under the then-default confidence engine idws (developed by his mentor AJ) revealed the root cause at a glance: a green “ghost stripe” torn through the middle of red territory — a corridor where the decision rule collapses and a far-away class wins by default. The cure was Old Bear’s own invention: the idcn engine, whose smooth inverse-distance blending closes the corridor by construction. This report reenacts that episode end-to-end on the engineered Claude20 “sandwich” dataset: idws fails exactly the six samples planted in the corridor (96.8%, NmisP=6/188) while idcn classifies every sample correctly (100%, NmisP=0/188) — same data, same projection, only the lens changed.

1.The Problem Surfaces in the Field

The first sign of trouble came not from a validation report but from the company’s field application engineers. Deployed instruments were returning predictions that contradicted themselves: genuine LDPE samples flagged as PVC, while other LDPE samples — some closer to the LDPE center, some farther from it — passed without complaint. From the field’s vantage point there were no class maps, no decision surfaces, no theory: only samples and verdicts. Figure 1 recreates exactly that view.

2.A Fresh Lens Finds the Root Cause

As it happened, Old Bear was at that time developing a class-map visualization tool — modeled on the highly commercial graphing package SigmaPlot — that could paint every classifier’s decision as colored territory over the canonical-variate plane. He aimed the fresh tool at the troublesome dataset under idws, the confidence engine then shipping as the default, developed by his mentor AJ. What the map revealed was the root cause in a single frame: a green ghost stripe slicing through the middle of red territory (Figure 2). Every misclassified sample from the field sat inside that stripe.

The mechanism, in plain language: imagine three neighborhoods on a map — Gray (HDPE), Red (LDPE), and Green (PVC). To decide which neighborhood a new house belongs to, the engine says: the closer you are to a neighborhood’s center, the more confident that neighborhood’s claim. The question is how fast confidence fades as you walk away. idws sets Red’s fade rate by glancing at whichever other neighborhood happens to be nearest to where you are standing. In one corridor of the map, that nearest “rival” is Gray — and because Gray and Red centers sit close together, idws concludes Red’s influence must die off almost instantly there. Inside that corridor, Red’s confidence collapses so fast that far-away Green wins by default: a green ghost stripe appears in the middle of red land, and any real sample unlucky enough to live there is condemned as green.

REDmain LDPE + boundary huggers ✓
GREENghost stripe · 6 LDPE ✗ → PVC
REDsandwich · real LDPE ✓ (farther from red!)
GREENmain PVC, 5.6 CV away

3.The Fix: Inventing idcn

Diagnosis in hand, Old Bear’s answer was again his own: a new confidence engine, idcn, that blends all rival classes smoothly by inverse-distance weighting instead of letting the single nearest rival dictate the fade rate. The blend never snaps, so the decision surface can never tear open a corridor — no ghost stripe, by construction. The proof is the same two views, re-run with nothing changed but the engine.

4.Behind the Reenactment: Engineering the Demonstration Dataset

The figures above are not the original field data — they are a modern reenactment, engineered so that the historical failure mode is impossible to miss. The starting point was the Claude17 extract dataset: 177 training and 183 prediction NIR spectra of three polymers (HDPE, LDPE, PVC) over 119 wavelengths. Run with norm1=0, asmc=0, decayfac=0.1, rule=conf, both confidence engines score a perfect 100% on it — yet the idws star-map already harbors a hair-thin green sliver at CV1 ≈ 9.3–10.6 (Figure 5): the same ghost-stripe artifact, present but harmless, because no sample happens to fall inside it. The engineering objective was to reshape the classes until the stripe sat wide, consequential, and at the red class’s doorstep — with genuine LDPE samples inside it — recreating in miniature exactly the situation the field engineers once stumbled into.

Step zero: cloning the referee

Guesswork against a 4,700-line program is hopeless, so the first move was a faithful Python port of the entire decision chain: uncentered PCA, the cancv_m4 cross-validation that selects canopcfac, CDA whitening, and the confidence formula CF = 100·post·exp(−(gv−dsb)/(iddf·decayfac)) with both iddf variants. The port reproduced the baseline exactly: canopcfac=7, both engines 0/183, ghost stripe in the same place to the pixel. Every subsequent design decision was rehearsed thousands of times in this sandbox before MATLAB ever saw a file — which is why the final verification ran clean on the first attempt.

Three-stage dataset engineering

Stage 1 — Claude18 “idwsTrap”: proof of concept. Pulling the PVC mean 25% toward LDPE (plus a shear) and shifting HDPE moved the stripe next to the red cloud and widened it four-fold. Six planted samples — each a genuine LDPE prediction spectrum plus a small blend of class-mean directions, solved to land exactly on chosen map coordinates — were misclassified as PVC by idws (6/189) and correctly classified by idcn (0/189). Their goodv ≈ 2 (threshold 25): by every screening measure they are ordinary LDPE.

Stage 2 — Claude19 “idwsTrapX”: to the theoretical limit. Strengthening the pull (α=0.60, Gray–Red Mahalanobis distance down to 1.52) drove the stripe’s left edge to 3.8 CV-units from the red centroid — nearly touching the no-decay radius √χ²=3.04, the mathematical floor. Eight real LDPE samples were shepherded to hug the boundary, shrinking the visible gap between the last correct red sample and the first condemned star to 0.29 CV-units.

Stage 3 — Claude20 “idwsSandwich”: the four-band contradiction. Reflecting PVC’s left tail (λ=−0.30) — Old Bear’s own idea — skewed the class rightward: the nearest green sample retreated 5.6 CV-units beyond the sandwich, while the whitened LDPE–PVC distance swelled to 14.7, widening the sandwich band to 0.36 CV — enough to paint solid red at map resolution for any grid alignment (verified for every phase). Four real LDPE samples were relocated into the sandwich; every marker passed a ±0.1 box test guaranteeing all four engines (idws/idcn sample engines and both map-grid engines) agree throughout the surrounding map cell. Walking away from the red centroid, the verdicts flip three times: boundary huggers at 5.9 → red ✓; planted stars at 6.1–6.2 → green ✗; sandwich samples at 6.8–6.9 — farther still — → red ✓. Finally, per request, prediction row 66 (the first sandwich sample) was removed, yielding the shipped rmP66 / nsampP188 file. All figures in Sections 1–3 are screenshots from CDA_mapstar_Merge_new.m itself — not from the Python sandbox — and every number matched the pre-registered prediction on the first run.

5.The Instrument, Upgraded

The same session also upgraded the viewing instrument itself — the modern descendant of that original SigmaPlot-inspired tool. CDA_mapstar_Merge_new.m and its front end CDA_mapstar_gui_new.m gained three clarity features: (a) the map grid increment increm and the class-region transparency alpha are now exposed as GUI spinners (previously locked at 0.2 and hard-wired at 0.3); (b) a new display dropdown offers a points-only mode (inp.pointsonly=1) that suppresses the region fill and the white star contours entirely — and skips the expensive map-grid computation altogether — leaving just the Tset/Pset markers and the yellow misPred rings on a gridded white background; and (c) the Pset “+” markers are drawn with a much bolder stroke, so predictions no longer vanish against the tinted regions. The two housekeeping checkboxes (close the intermediate Tset map, export CDAmodel/CDApredict) moved into the program as internal settings, and every GUI font shrank 20% to make room — the window now hosts nine option rows in less space than the old eight. It is these upgrades that made the storytelling of Sections 1–3 possible: the points-only mode recreates the field’s map-less vantage point, and the fine grid renders the ghost stripe crisply at the pixel level.

Take-Home Message

A perfect accuracy score can hide a broken decision rule — and the field will find it before the lab does. idws and idcn tie at 100% on the original data, yet idws carries a structural discontinuity: its confidence decay rate is dictated by whichever rival class is momentarily nearest, so the decision surface can tear open a false-color corridor where no data has ever been. Once samples legitimately occupy that corridor, idws fails them while idcn — whose inverse-distance blending is smooth by construction — does not. The historical sequence told here is the deeper lesson: the contradiction surfaced as raw verdicts in the field (Figure 1); a purpose-built visualization tool converted those verdicts into a visible root cause (Figure 2); and the fix was a new algorithm designed around the diagnosis (Figures 3–4). Predictions flipping correct → wrong → correct as one walks away from the class centroid is an ordering no sane distance-based classifier should produce. When benchmarking classifiers, probe the geometry of the decision surface, not just the headline accuracy.

8.Appendix: Reproduction Recipe & Deliverables

inp.norm1 = 0;  inp.asmc = 0;  inp.decayfac = 0.1;
inp.increm = 0.2;  inp.predrule = 'conf';
inp.sinterd = 'idws';  % then repeat with 'idcn'

Note: the filename carries no _norm1 token, so the program default norm1=1 would silently apply — norm1=0 must be set explicitly. The series is tuned to the program-selected canopcfac=7 (selection margin 29.87 vs 29.25 cvpct, no tie ambiguity) and is not intended to be robust at other PC counts. Deliverables: four .mat files (Claude18_idwsTrap, Claude19_idwsTrapX, Claude20_idwsSandwich nsampP189 and nsampP188), before/after map figures, zoom details, and this report. File format follows the Atrainpketc convention throughout: labels 1–3, AclassinfoT/P stored as double, clistclslabel = {'HDPE','LDPE','PVC'}, planted rows tagged LDPE_planted01–06 in AclabelP.
